text:
A: Hiya! Can you hear me alright? Jaspal, Derby.
B: Hiya! Yeah, I can hear you. I'm Gemma, I'm in Beeston, but I'm Derby born, so you're practically family.
A: Gemma! Right, I've got to tell you this. I had a call with Craig, Warrington lad, and he said he'd spoken to a physio called Gemma with a dog called Biscuit. And my partner is a physio called Gemma, and we've got a dog called Biscuit.
B: Shut up. You're joking.
A: Swear down. So for about ten seconds I thought she'd joined the study and married a Dan behind my back.
B: (laughs) Oh my God. I am married to a Dan! Is your Gemma at Nottingham?
A: No, Royal Derby. Cocker spaniel, old boy, eats socks. Yours?
B: Cockapoo, chews phone chargers. So we're different Gemmas, you're safe. That's honestly mad though. Is she MSK?
A: Yeah, MSK. She'll probably know you, to be fair, it's a small world, physios.
B: It really is. Tell her the Beeston Gemma says hi. And that the waiting list's from hell over here as well.
A: Oh, she says the same, word for word. Comes in after a long shift and just lies on the settee going "don't talk to me".
B: That's me after a ten-hour clinic! I get home and lie on the floor with Biscuit. So what do you do? Let me guess, teacher, with all the textbooks?
A: Everyone gets that. Sixth form college, Business and Economics, on the edge of Derby. I run Young Enterprise as well, so the kids make stuff and try and sell it. Last year's lot did candles and they actually turned a profit, which I'll take full credit for, obviously.
B: (laughs) Obviously. See, I'd love to know about business stuff. I want my own clinic eventually, private physio and Pilates, nice fit-out, proper Instagram, be my own boss, do you know what I mean?
A: Do it. Honestly. Half my job is telling seventeen-year-olds they can run a business, so I'd be a hypocrite if I said don't. What's stopping you?
B: Erm, money, mainly. And I'm going for a Band 7 first. I'm doing private massage on Saturdays to build up clients, sort of thing.
A: That's sensible, that's the proper way. I've got a half-built idea for a tutoring company, and by half-built I mean it's a note on my phone.
B: (laughs) That counts! Where in Derby did you grow up?
A: Littleover now, but we came over when I was nine, from Kabul via Delhi. Uncle had a shop on Normanton Road. Where were you?
B: Allenton. Me mum and dad are still there. I went to sixth form in Derby, first in the family to go to uni, so me mum still tells everyone at the Co-op.
A: Ha, my mum's the same, she tells the whole gurdwara I'm basically running the college. I'm not, for the record. Do you still go to Pride Park?
B: Now and again, with me dad. More for the day out, if I'm honest, the pie and that. He had a heart scare last year, so I like taking him when I can.
A: Yeah. That's nice, that. Is he doing alright?
B: He's much better, thanks. He moans about the board the whole way home, so he must be.
A: That's how you know they're healthy, mate. Moaning about the board is the best medicine going.
